sections.html:
• Other names: Javanese snails, Susuh Kura snails
  • Optimal tank size: 10 gallons (~40 litres)
  • Size: up to 7.5 cm
  • Optimal temperature: 26 – 32°C
  • Optimal pH: 7.0 – 8.5
  • Optimal GH: 6 – 15
  • Nitrate: less than 60 ppm
  • Diet: algae eater/omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Lifespan: up to 5 years
  • Colour: dark brown to black

• Size: up to 7.5 cm; average shell length 2.5 – 5 cm.
  • Shell: variable, turreted or elongate conic, spire angle about 30 degrees, smooth surface, narrow and shallow suture, usually 7 to 9 flattened whorls. In adults the apex is often completely eroded.
  • Operculum: oval with 3 to 4 whorls increasing in diameter.
  • Aperture: oval with a straight outer lip.
  • Shell colour: dark brown to black, or yellowish to brown, often with brownish flames.
  • Body colour: head and foot usually dark grey to black; mantle edge dark grey or palely pigmented; head, tentacles and neck dark grey to black.
  • Lifespan: no data for the wild; with proper care the expected average is 3 to 5 years.

Sulcospira testudinaria is endemic to Indonesia with a wide distribution across freshwater habitats, particularly prevalent on the island of Java.

It can be observed in various locations such as Central Java (Code River, Pegunungan Sewu), West Java (Bogor, Jakarta, Cikeruh River), and East Java (Meru Betiri National Park, the Brantas River).

In their natural habitat, Black Panther Snails primarily occur in relatively fast-running waters, such as rivers, streams, or creeks. However, sometimes they can be found in lakes, and even irrigation canals of rice fields.

In their natural environment, they inhabit rivers with sandy, muddy, and rocky substrates.

The minimum recommended tank size is 10 gallons (40 litres). These snails need a lot of room to crawl, eat, and explore.

If the tank is smaller, you may have feeding problems unless you supplement their diet, as there may not be sufficient algae and biofilm to sustain them.

Care is quite easy and straightforward. They are low-maintenance and can withstand varied ranges of water parameters. According to a study, Sulcospira testudinaria is quite tolerant of even polluted waters.

It is important to cycle your tank before bringing snails home, then check water quality with a test kit.

Acclimation: avoid placing them directly into the tank, as sudden changes can harm them. Acclimate gradually, as with all invertebrates, and do it very slowly to prevent unnecessary stress.

• Temperature: these snails require warm water. In nature they live at around 30°C, so the optimal aquarium temperature is 26 – 32°C. They may sometimes be found at 22 – 24°C, which is not ideal.
  • pH: aim for 7.0 – 8.5. They do not like acidic water (below 7.0), which slowly dissolves their shell, making it fragile.
  • Hardness: 6 – 15 GH. Harder water benefits their shells.
  • Dissolved oxygen: >6 mg/l.
  • Salinity: a freshwater snail that does not tolerate salinity well. It usually retracts into the shell and regains activity immediately when moved to freshwater.

Aeration and flow: in nature they inhabit shallow streams and rivers with moderate or even fast current. They are morphologically suited to stream life and need high oxygen levels. They can be kept without a strong current, but ample oxygen supply is essential.

• Lighting: no special requirements. The snails are nocturnal, so lighting should be adapted to the needs of plants (and/or algae if needed).
  • Filtration: no special requirements. A filter suited to the tank size is enough.
  • Substrate: they can be kept with any substrate, but smooth gravel is a better choice, as algae grows more easily on it. These snails do not burrow much or deeply, so soil or sand substrates are unnecessary.
  • Decorations: driftwood, PVC pipes, leaves, rocks, live plants, fake plants and other decorations offer ample surface area for algae and biofilm, so any decor is a good choice.

These snails are omnivorous and great scavengers. According to a study, Black Panther Snails can reduce the total organic matter in waste by up to 87%. They are not a total substitute for tank maintenance, but will help keep the tank clean.

In aquariums, their diet consists mainly of grazing on:

  • detritus,
  • biofilm,
  • various types of algae (including diatoms (brown algae), Green spot algae, Green Dust Algae)

The author supplements their diet with vegetables and commercial foods. They will eat the same food you feed your fish and shrimp (flakes, algae wafers, pellets, and granules).

Important: calcium plays a huge role in snails. It is needed for several vital life processes, the most obvious being the formation of shells.

  • Diet type: omnivore
  • Feeding frequency: 1 – 2 times a week

Safe in planted tanks? The author found no mention of these snails consuming live and healthy plants, so there should be no issues in planted aquariums.

Black Panther Snails are completely non-aggressive by nature. They have only their operculum (trap-door) and shell for protection.

These snails are not obligate diggers. Although they can burrow in soft substrates, they generally do not move under it.

They are nocturnal: during the night they crawl on the surface and may hide during the day. Nocturnal behaviour is not uncommon for grazing invertebrates and is mainly associated with avoiding visual predators whilst feeding.

  • Social: yes
  • Activity level: average
  • Peaceful: yes
  • Burrowers: yes

Suitable tankmates: these snails are completely harmless and fit any peaceful community tank if tankmates share similar water preferences.

  • Fish: Danio rerio, Endlers, Least Killifish, Brilliant Rummynose Tetras, Southern platyfish, Pygmy Swordtail, Ghost Glass Catfish, Medaka Ricefish, etc.
  • Shrimp: species that prefer slightly alkaline water, e.g. Vampire shrimp, Bamboo Shrimp, Amano Shrimp, Ghost shrimp, Cherry shrimp, Blue tiger shrimp, Snowball shrimp, Caridina cf. babaulti, Blue Velvet Shrimp, Malawa Shrimp.
  • Snails: any freshwater snails, except Assassin snails.
  • Avoid: all crayfish (even Dwarf Mexican crayfish), most freshwater crabs, predatory shrimp such as Macrobrachium (Red Claw Shrimp, Whisker shrimp, etc.), and snail-eating fish such as puffers, including Dwarf puffers.

Very little is known about the life cycle requirements of these snails. The following is from scientific literature:

  • Sulcospira testudinaria is not a hermaphrodite species.
  • Females are fertilized internally.
  • They are viviparous.
  • On average, females can produce 100 to 150 similarly-sized embryonic shells.
  • After hatching, the embryo is about 1.00 mm in length.

It is currently unknown how the sexes differ, as well as the gestation period and the rate at which they reach sexual maturity.

Etymology: the genus name "Sulcospira" derives from the Latin "Sulcus" (groove) and "Spira" (spiral). The species name "testudinaria" derives from New Latin "Testudo" (tortoise) and "-aria" (relating to), so it can be read as resembling a tortoise.

Taxonomy: Animalia; Mollusca; Gastropoda; Prosobranchia; Caenogastropoda; family Pachychilidae (river snails); genus Sulcospira. Sulcospira is one of the oldest taxonomically recognized genera of Pachychilidae but also one of the most poorly known.

Drawbacks: these snails are highly heat-loving and prefer relatively strong currents; they resemble Black devil snails; and as they age the apex of the shell is often completely eroded, significantly affecting their ornamented appearance.

  • Adharini, Ratih Ida, and Putri Latifa Arumsari. "Structure and Distribution of Macrobenthos Community in Code River, Yogyakarta, Indonesia." Indonesian Journal of Limnology 2, no. 2 (2021): 21-27.
